title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentThe friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentThe friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after",  she said she "was just crying - really upset".The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually."He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her."He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.She said the woman replied "lots of times"."She told me that she was in a lot of pain" and that "she couldn't sit down".Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court.From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape.She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess"."She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone".The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her. "I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police. "She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it."She told jurors: "She didn't think she would be believed, and she didn't think it would be worth it to go."She kind of put it behind her."Statements from the alleged rape victim's parents said their daughter stayed with them for about two months after the alleged incident with Brand. Her mother's statement said: "I just remember her saying 'he raped me'."She was very worried about HIV," she said, adding that her daughter had started talking about it during a car journey."She said she went to his place, went to see him, as she had always admired him."Her father recalled their daughter being "very upset and very unwell", during the stay, that that she was "upset by something that had happened to her."The father said in his statement that his daughter told him: "They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted."I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said 'no' several times."I said 'you have been raped, that's rape'."He said his daughter got a sexual health check, and he said he had only recently learned his daughter is accusing Brand of anal rape.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears

title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
description: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, feari
body: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid."With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS NOW, external. In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation. The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out." Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed."We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one. She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating. Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it"."You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

schema.headline: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out

title: New York City reconsiders a classic attraction: are horse-drawn carriages abuse?
description: After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most f
body: After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horses, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried."What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old about her current horse, Starlight. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?"Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity.On Thursday, New York City Council is expected to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry.But several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban."There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing."Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions. New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers. But the ban movement found new momentum this summer.In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park.Several Central Park horse carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk.Lawson, who was nearby on the day Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic". But she said if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years.The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision.Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation."They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals."Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke."I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way."Fidan said he was angry, and that officials were passing a ban without talking in-person to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked.The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment.The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling, and financial compensation for those in the business.A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (£ 44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing.But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the plan did not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out".The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year. The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work.Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' well-being have been raised in the city for decades.The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. In 1866, after Henry Bergh witnessed the brutal beating of a carriage horse, he established the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) to protest horses' treatment and other instances of animal abuse.People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and a coalition of organisations supporting the horse-carriage ban also oppose the carriages.Horses can work up to nine hours a day. They are currently restricted to certain entrances of the park, where they stand and wait with drivers to be hired. Customers pay $72.22 for a 20-minute ride, plus $28.89 for every extra ten minutes.Vanessa Stolle, a German tourist, said she and her family had horses at home - and that they do not belong in a noisy park pulling passengers."To stand the whole day here – it's loud for them and they can't go to the countryside," she said.A fellow German tourist, Christian Bauers, disagreed. He remembered seeing the horses when he came to Central Park 20 years ago. "It's part of the culture of New York," he said. "Let them stay. It's cute."Jeanne Collopy is an animal lover from Colorado, where horses run wild, she said. She worries about accidents in the park that have harmed humans and horses."I know there's a union and I hate to have people out of work," she said, adding: "It's a little bit confining for the horses."Her husband, Chris Koenigs, said the animals were "wonderful" to look at. But the death of the teenager this summer was "sickening", and a high price to pay for enjoying the horses, he said."The park is magnificent,"  he added. "I can't help but think, it would be a magnificent park with or without the carriages."

schema.headline: New York City reconsiders a classic attraction: are horse-drawn carriages abuse?

title: Bridgend man, 61, charged with murder after 'stabbed' woman dies following crash
description: A man has been charged with murder after a woman who had suffered "stab wounds" died following a crash.Housing association worker Eleanor Barnfield, 4
body: A man has been charged with murder after a woman who had suffered "stab wounds" died following a crash.Housing association worker Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.Clifford Foster, 61, from Bridgend, has been charged with murder and is due to appear at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday.The Welsh Ambulance Service (WAS) has denied Barnfield was driving because of ambulance wait times, saying it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online.It said medics were called to the crash in Coity Road at about 12:44 BST and a response unit arrived seven minutes later.In a statement issued later on Thursday, WAS said that from initial investigations it had been "unable to identify" any calls from Barnfield's phone numbers."Enquiries are ongoing to establish if any calls were received by other means," it added.Reports in some media had claimed Eleanor had crashed her car while driving herself to hospital.Ger-y-Nant retirement housing complex, where police arrested Foster on Tuesday, is a few minutes' drive from the Princess of Wales Hospital, with Coity Road the main road in between.Senior Investigating Officer Claire Lamerton said her thoughts were with Barnfield's loved ones, who were being supported by specialist officers."This is not being investigated as a domestic incident, and I encourage the public to not speculate about the circumstances as court proceedings are now active," she said.

schema.headline: Bridgend man, 61, charged with murder after 'stabbed' woman dies following crash

title: Retired Woking decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
description: A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction. The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the car
body: A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction. The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than £6,000.His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for £1.56m. The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record. "I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified."When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school. "I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment."He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."Pokémon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay. One set which cost him £300 at the time went for £75,000 at Wednesday's auction. The cards, all filed into bespoke Pokémon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the franchise.

schema.headline: Retired Woking decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m

title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
description: Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.The banking group said 1,000 posts h
body: Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce. The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year."It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said."Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said."It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce"."Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme  focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.Barclays also revealed it made £2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business."AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future."We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake."Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers. Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years"."Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further £1.1bn of savings in 2027.

schema.headline: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI

title: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad
description: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadImage caption, Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseasByElizabeth
body: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadImage caption, Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseasByElizabeth AndersonBusiness reporterLast year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place."I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey, external of 15,000 final year university students.Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high. UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report, external.For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?Australia: 'The weather's beautiful, even in the winter'While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show., externalIn addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme,, external British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.Image source, Rachel JamesImage caption, Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than LondonRachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched."People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."The US: 'I'm paid a lot more here'Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures, external from the UK's Office for National Statistics.It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.Image source, Charlie WestImage caption, Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunitiesCharlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching."I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live."In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."Europe: 'If you can work across the EU there are more opportunities'The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.Image source, Owein IvesonImage caption, Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from FinlandThis is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020."Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon."To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas. "When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London. "I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Let us know

schema.headline: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad

title: Women take to social media to break the taboo of UTIs
description: "The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells
body: "The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells her roughly 8,000 followers in a video on TikTok.For nearly five years, Adrianne has lived with a chronic urinary tract infection (UTI) - a condition it took her two years to get a diagnosis for.In that time she was wrongly told it was colon cancer, Crohn's disease or even that her partner must have been cheating and had given her a sexually transmitted infection.What started as one UTI in 2022 became a debilitating cycle."It has completely stripped me of everything: being able to work properly, my relationships, my friendships, going out, being able to have a normal social life," says Adrianne, who works in digital marketing in London.The 29-year-old was eventually diagnosed privately with a chronic UTI - something experts estimate could affect up to 1.7 million women in the UK, external. Men and children are also affected.Adrianne is not alone in sharing her story and coping mechanisms on social media to fight the stigma surrounding UTIs.A quick search on Tiktok or Instagram shows hundreds of posts of women of all ages talking about the reality of living with recurrent and chronic UTIs."I felt incredibly nervous to put myself out there, but there's now this community of people who can share tips with each other, and understand each other," said Adrianne, saying her posts have had a "really positive response"."It's very validating."While sending a urine sample to the lab remains the gold standard to diagnose a UTI, "false negatives" can often occur, says Professor Chris Harding, a consultant urologist at Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.Another hurdle is the significant crossover between chronic UTIs and other conditions such as painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic pain and endometriosis, says Magda Kujawa, a consultant urologist at Stockport NHS Foundation Trust.Adrianne says she felt "dismissed" by doctors while trying to get a diagnosis, and frustrated at repeatedly being given advice around hygiene and hydration, while her symptoms persisted.Both experts say health professionals should listen to the patient's story to understand whether symptoms amount to a recurrent or chronic condition or something else entirely.Since she started posting online, Adrianne has received messages from other young women who worry they are "dirty" and "not taking care of themselves" or that there is "something wrong with them". "There's definitely still a lot of stigma around why people get them (UTIs), and it all just comes back to education. We're not taught about them at school," she adds.Laura Von Müllen, 26, has also been diagnosed with a chronic UTI and documents her experience on TikTok.She says her symptoms "really badly" impacted university, and became particularly difficult to manage when she started working. She now works remotely from Kent doing social media management.As well as urinary symptoms, Laura says she also experiences heart palpitations and panic attacks."People don't understand, they think it's just a UTI and that it'll clear within three days, but I've still got mine two years later," she says.Laura also feels there is still a lot of misconception around UTIs. "People have said to me: who have you been sleeping with then? When that's not the case."Adrianne and Laura hope more women sharing their experience will help demystify the condition.Harding agrees. adding that "the more we can talk about these conditions, the more people will present to appropriate specialists and get the right treatment."But both Harding and Kujawa warn that while social media can be a useful resource, there is the risk of coming across misinformation and harmful advice, including "hacks" that could cause more harm. "I've seen women on social media sitting in baths of disinfectant, all because they were convinced that that they were dirty, and that's why they were getting infections. And actually, that just made things ten times worse," Kujawa says.While Adrianne and Laura's symptoms are showing improvements, they say it's a "long road to recovery".

schema.headline: Women take to social media to break the taboo of UTIs

title: Michael Carrick: Man Utd boss carrying on as Old Trafford club eyes possible replacements
description: Michael Carrick is set to remain in charge of Manchester United for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, but senior figures are concerne
body: Michael Carrick is set to remain in charge of Manchester United for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, but senior figures are concerned about performances and results.Carrick is said to be carrying on as normal and has not been made aware of any imminent change following Wednesday's humiliating 4-1 defeat by Italian side Como.But some at Old Trafford believe the squad should be doing much better, with one source telling BBC Sport: "We need to work hard to get through it."Another accepted the level of current injuries "doesn't help, but no excuse", claiming effort levels were "concerning"."We have a Champions League squad and need to be playing at that level," the source said.Despite concern at the performances, some in the United hierachy are of the view chopping and changing mangers so regularly in recent years has failed to arrest United's decline, and Carrick has been let down by players who are under-performing.While club sources say Carrick will remain in charge for Sunday's match, United have already begun the process of identifying possible replacements.Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann are understood to have their eyes on the Old Trafford job.After Wednesday's match - United's seventh in a row without a win - captain Bruno Fernandes questioned Carrick's tactics.The players were given Thursday off but will be back at Carrington on Friday when Carrick will hold his news conference to preview the Bournemouth match at 1330 BST.While there remains major uncertainty over Carrick future, there is also an appreciation in some quarters of the progress he and his squad made last season, and a view he should be given more time to turn things around.For weeks, managers - in and out of work - have grown aware the United job may become available.Howe, for example, is available and would be considered. Sources have indicated the former Newcastle boss is open to returning to management with United after leaving St James' Park in the close season.Former Chelsea boss Conte and ex-Germany manager Naglesmann, who are also out of work, are also interested.Aston Villa head coach Unai Emery and Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler's stock is high with those in the corridors of power at United - but extracting them from their respective clubs would be difficult.For the third year in a row, United have publicly and financially backed a manager in the summer, but positive results have not followed.Ruben Amorim staggered on to January, but the shock League Cup defeat at League Two side Grimsby last August and the awful performance at Brentford less than a month later stripped away his safety net and gave United's hierarchy nowhere to go when he attacked their influence.United looked extensively at other candidates, including Thomas Tuchel and Roberto de Zerbi, in the summer of 2024 before deciding to stick with Erik ten Hag. The Dutchman was dismissed in the October.Now, we have Carrick.There were dissenting voices when he was appointed on a permanent basis in May, but the majority of supporters felt 12 wins from 17 in interim charge and a place in the Champions League after a two-year absence meant the 45-year-old former United midfielder deserved a crack at the job.But, as ever, results shape everything.There are numerous reasons behind the club's poor form this season and blame can be apportioned across a variety of departments and to the very top of the club. However, the brutal truth is two wins from 11 games, and none in seven, their worst run since 2015-16 when eight matches without a win took Louis van Gaal to the brink of dismissal, is simply not good enough. And as head coach, Carrick bears significant responsibility for that.Accusations of a lack of passion, desire and intensity have dogged United all season, having won just two of their matches in all competitions.The team have also been hampered by injuries and players failing to reach the level anticipated.While they have struggled in attack, they have also only kept a single clean sheet all season as form, results and confidence have all dipped.Mixed into that negativity has come explosive post-match comments from experienced defender Lisandro Martinez, attacking the recruitment, and Fernandes, attacking Carrick and his tactics. In between was the interview in the Athletic with Ten Hag when he spoke of 'broken promises' and a 'toxic culture'. It all smacks of a club lacking control, discipline and a clear forward-looking strategy.There is certainly a view from senior figures around the club that while overall recruitment can be questioned - specifically strengthening midfield in the summer at the expense of bringing in striking support for Benjamin Sesko or competition at left-back  - the players have to take a significant amount of responsibility.Whether that helps Carrick is another matter.The proximity of United's next Premier League game does not make immediate change straightforward, even if that was the thinking.Following Amorim's dismissal in January, former United midfielder Darren Fletcher took over as interim manager for two games. Fletcher subsequently returned to his role as Under-18 coach, but two of the coaches who helped him, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, stayed with the senior set-up as part of Carrick's team.United have a clear midweek coming up following their EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, who came back from two down to win at Old Trafford last month. That, in theory, would allow time to take stock without the immediate pressure a match can bring.Bournemouth secured their first Premier League win under new boss Marco Rose last week. They drew 4-4 in a memorable encounter at Old Trafford last season, prior to that, they won 3-0 on both of their previous two visits.It remains to be seen if Carrick will be in charge, and if so, how long after that.It seems the only certainty around Manchester United just now, is the sense of uncertainty - again.

schema.headline: Michael Carrick: Man Utd boss carrying on as Old Trafford club eyes possible replacements

title: Caroline Flack's brother never recovered, inquest hears
description: The brother of TV presenter Caroline Flack took his own life having "never recovered" after his sister's death, an inquest heard.Paul Flack, 55, was f
body: The brother of TV presenter Caroline Flack took his own life having "never recovered" after his sister's death, an inquest heard.Paul Flack, 55, was found unresponsive at his home in Sandringham Road, Norwich, on 21 June, and died later in hospital.His partner told Norfolk Coroner's Court how he had struggled with his father developing dementia and his younger sister's death in 2020.Area Coroner Johanna Thompson gave a narrative conclusion, stating Paul Flack died while under the influence of alcohol and that his "intent in doing so is unknown".He was described as "everyone's favourite person" by his partner Joanna Millington, but she said this "took its toll".His sister, the ex-Love Island and X Factor host, was found dead at her home in Stoke Newington, east London, on 15 February 2020."We then went into lockdown for Covid," said Millington, who provided a written statement to the court."I do not think Paul ever recovered from this."An inquest later established Caroline Flack took her own life, aged 40, having feared press intrusion ahead of her trial accused of assaulting her boyfriend.

schema.headline: Caroline Flack's brother never recovered, inquest hears

title: Emergency powers planned to protect UK's undersea cables
description: The government has outlined new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables amid increased fears of Russian interference.Ministers are set t
body: The government has outlined new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables amid increased fears of Russian interference.Ministers are set to gain powers to order telecom companies to remove or disable services during national security emergencies, as well as granting officials access to sites including cable landing stations.The government has also outlined plans for stronger criminal penalties for those convicted of tampering with either undersea internet cables or energy pipelines. The new powers would be backed up with prison sentences of up to 14 years for intentional conduct, 10 years for reckless conduct and two years for grossly negligent conduct, alongside unlimited fines.It comes amid growing fears of suspicious activity in UK waters, and concerns that legal powers over the network have not kept pace with its growing importance to national security.An extensive network of undersea cables and pipelines owned and operated primarily by the private sector are thought to carry almost all the UK's international data traffic and three-quarters of its gas supplies.The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report last year, external to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.The UK and its Nato allies are concerned about the risk Russia poses to offshore infrastructure. In April, the government accused Russian submarines of conducting a covert operation over cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK. The UK has also accused Russia of mapping undersea infrastructure using spy ships. Last year, it revealed the Royal Navy had tracked one such suspected ship, the Yantar, after it passed near UK waters. Russia has denied the claims, and accused the UK of stirring up tensions through "anti-Russian alarmism". In a policy paper on Thursday, the government said it currently lacked emergency powers to deal with incidents affecting undersea infrastructure.It added there were currently no equivalent powers to measures that allow intervention in the water and air traffic sectors, whilst broader powers for national emergencies could prove too slow to exercise during a crisis.It is now proposing new powers that would allow it to force telecoms companies to hand over information or modify or disable services in connection with specific threats or incidents.The changes will require new legislation, to be set out after a consultation with industry closing in January.Companies that refused to comply with the orders could be fined up to £17m or 10% of global turnover. The orders would typically be published, but could be made secret on national security grounds, it added.The proposed powers are not intended to apply to companies operating energy infrastructure,  although the document added that new powers in this area were being considered separately.Ministers said they hoped the new powers would apply across the "full extent" of undersea services, including outside the UK's territorial waters, which extend up to 12 nautical miles from the coast.However, the document concedes this is likely to require co-ordination with other countries, adding that the government was considering how its proposals compare to equivalent regimes internationally. It was also uncertain that existing laws on undersea infrastructure, dating from the Victorian period and designed for telegraphic cables, could be used for breaches of modern fibre-optic cables, the document added.

schema.headline: Emergency powers planned to protect UK's undersea cables

title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
description: I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built.We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed duri
body: I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built.We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction.In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building.The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet.There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025.But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution.Less than two months ago, 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI.It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant.The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit.One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult.However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI.The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix.It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked. From that point the clock started ticking. As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site."There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University."How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers?"Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out."But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made. We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either.As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success. Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story. "We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4."We have enormous capability to handle these risks."But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in.Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first.For many it may be a significant repair job, so if there's a web developer in your life you may want to send them thoughts, prayers and maybe a strong coffee.

schema.headline: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb

title: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
description: Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across
body: Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend. Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday."The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations."In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the Rhône prefecture said in a statement.Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests. Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy".In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron. The Élysée Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice.Nuñez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

schema.headline: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron

title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
description: Figure caption, Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war ragesByOrla GuerinSenior International CorrespondentReporting fromA
body: Figure caption, Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war ragesByOrla GuerinSenior International CorrespondentReporting fromAdenFrom the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden."It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."Image caption, The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.Image caption, More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN saysMalnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast,  and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.Image caption, Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother LinaWe followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018."I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred."I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."Image caption, Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutritionAs we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor."It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says. "We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.Image caption, Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatmentThe malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon."Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics."Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.Image caption, Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the streetMany parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

schema.headline: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
